anger.title: Steady Under Pressure
anger.eyebrow_track: FOR EVERY MAN, ON EITHER TRACK
anger.lead: Twelve short films on steadiness under pressure: notice the surge early, buy six seconds, repair the same day, and build habits that hold.
anger.desc: Twelve short sessions on steadiness: the surge, early cues, six seconds, the exhale, the step away, naming it, the short apology, and steady habits.
anger.fine1: Self-paced. Twelve weeks. One short film each week, then a checkpoint and a lived practice. A Certified Facilitator is available when your seat is claimed.
anger.fine2: Completion never requires contact with your child. No practice asks you to go beyond the rules that govern you now or any court order.
anger.disclaimer: Not anger management, batterer intervention, or a substitute for any court-mandated program. Not designed or validated for those purposes and never ordered in their place.

welcome.title: Start here
welcome.ken: If you are a father under pressure, this is for you. Not a speech about never getting angry. Steadiness is a skill. It is how you keep your word when the heat comes, at home, at work, in a program. I have spent my life with men who want to be that father. This course trains the first move: notice the surge before it runs you.
welcome.micah: I built this path so you can finish it. Each week is one short film, a few questions, and a small practice you can actually do. I will walk it with you. No hour of sitting. One skill, then you go live your week. Here's session one.

sessions.title: The Surge Is a Signal
sessions.quote: The surge is a signal, not an order.
sessions.scene: The noise at a group meal rises. Voices overlap. His jaw sets before he knows why. That jaw is the earliest cue, and it is not an order to blow.
sessions.in_room: The body's stress response in plain language. You learn that the surge fires before deliberation, and that the skill is what you do in the next few seconds.
sessions.leave_with: You can treat the surge as information instead of a command.
sessions.practice: Log three moments of rising tension this week. For each, write the trigger and the earliest body cue you noticed.
sessions.science: The surge chemistry of stress fires before awareness; early cues give you a choice.

sessions.title: Know Your Early Cues
sessions.quote: Catch it in the jaw, not the shout.
sessions.scene: He used to notice only when his voice was already loud. Now he catches the heat in his face and the locked jaw two beats earlier. That gap is the whole game.
sessions.in_room: You map your personal early warning signs: jaw, fists, breath, tone, tunnel vision. You pick the two that show up first for you.
sessions.leave_with: You can name your earliest cues before the shout arrives.
sessions.practice: Write your top two early cues on a card. Check the card after three hard moments this week.
sessions.science: Body cues precede peak anger; naming them early widens the window to choose.

sessions.title: Six Seconds
sessions.quote: Six seconds buy your judgment back.
sessions.scene: The words are already loaded. He counts six silent seconds instead. The sentence he almost said stays unsaid, and the one he says next is his.
sessions.in_room: What happens in the seconds before a blowup, including the fast pathway that outruns judgment. The tool is a deliberate pause of about six seconds before you speak or act.
sessions.leave_with: You can insert six seconds when you feel the surge.
sessions.practice: Practice a six-second pause three times this week in real moments. Record the trigger and what you did after the pause.
sessions.science: A brief pause brings judgment back online after the fast threat pathway fires.

sessions.title: The Long Exhale
sessions.quote: A long exhale stands the body down.
sessions.scene: His chest is high and tight. He lengthens the out-breath once, slow. The shoulders drop a notch. He can hear himself think again.
sessions.in_room: Slow breathing with a longer exhale as a body-down tool you can run anywhere. You pair it with the six-second pause so the skill stacks.
sessions.leave_with: You can lower your own charge on demand with one long exhale.
sessions.practice: Run a daily long-exhale drill for five days. Use it once live under pressure and note what changed.
sessions.science: A long slow exhale signals the body to stand down faster than willpower alone.

sessions.title: Step Away to Come Back
sessions.quote: Step away to come back.
sessions.scene: Mid-argument on a call, his voice is climbing. He says he needs ten minutes and that he is coming back. He does, on time, quieter. The coming back is the skill.
sessions.in_room: Using a time-out on yourself as a reset, not a punishment. You practice leaving without abandoning the person or the topic.
sessions.leave_with: You can step away to cool down and return on time.
sessions.practice: Take one clean self time-out during a hard moment where you are now, then return when you said. Report both ends.
sessions.science: A clean break lets the body reset; the return keeps it from becoming abandonment.

sessions.title: The Line You Leave On
sessions.quote: Say the line, then leave the room.
sessions.scene: He almost storms out silent. Instead he says: I need ten minutes. I am coming back. Then he leaves. The room stays safer because the line held the door open.
sessions.in_room: You write and rehearse a short leave-line that names the break and the return time. No speech. No blame. Just the line, then the exit.
sessions.leave_with: You have a leave-line ready so a break is a reset, not a disappearance.
sessions.practice: Write your leave-line in under fifteen words. Rehearse it aloud three times. Use it once this week if needed.
sessions.science: Naming the return turns a break into a trustworthy pause.

sessions.title: Name the Feeling
sessions.quote: Say the feeling so you do not have to show it.
sessions.scene: Instead of the slammed cabinet, he says I am frustrated, and not at you. Five words. The temperature drops a degree, and the child hears the words too.
sessions.in_room: Putting feelings into words lowers their intensity. You practice naming your own state in plain language before it becomes a show.
sessions.leave_with: You can handle feelings by naming them instead of acting them out.
sessions.practice: Name one feeling out loud in three separate moments this week. Log the words you used.
sessions.science: Naming a feeling out loud measurably lowers its charge.

sessions.title: Feelings Without Weapons
sessions.quote: Name it without loading it.
sessions.scene: He almost says you always do this. He swaps it for I am angry and I want to finish this calmly. Same feeling. No weapon attached.
sessions.in_room: You strip blame, insults, and history dumps from the naming sentence. Clean naming lowers heat; loaded naming restarts the fight.
sessions.leave_with: You can name hard feelings without arming them.
sessions.practice: Rewrite two loaded sentences into clean feeling statements. Use one clean line live this week.
sessions.science: Blame reloads conflict; clean labeling keeps the skill usable.

sessions.title: Own It Same Day
sessions.quote: Own it out loud, same day.
sessions.scene: Last night he barked over nothing. This morning, before anything else: I was wrong to raise my voice. You did not deserve that. Same day. No wait.
sessions.in_room: Repair after a rupture protects the relationship. You practice owning the moment out loud the same day, specific and without excuses.
sessions.leave_with: You can own a bad moment the same day it happened.
sessions.practice: Write one ownership line for a recent miss. Deliver it same day if contact is allowed, or deliver a live ownership to someone where you are now.
sessions.science: Fast ownership keeps a rupture from hardening into the relationship's normal.

sessions.title: The Short Apology
sessions.quote: Short, specific, no defense.
sessions.scene: He starts to explain the week. He stops. He says only: I raised my voice at you. That was wrong. I will step away next time. Ten words. It lands.
sessions.in_room: You practice a short apology script: the specific act, that it was wrong, and one next step. Defense stays out.
sessions.leave_with: You can apologize short, specific, and without defense.
sessions.practice: Write a short apology for one real miss. Cut every excuse. Rehearse once aloud, then deliver if allowed.
sessions.science: Short specific repair lands; defense undoes it.

sessions.title: Sleep, Food, Movement
sessions.quote: Steadiness is built in the boring hours.
sessions.scene: Lights out at the same hour five nights straight, a walk or a workout most days, and by day five the fuse is longer. He can see it in his own log.
sessions.in_room: The daily regulators that raise your threshold: sleep, food, and movement. Willpower sits on top of a body that is fed and rested.
sessions.leave_with: You can lower baseline reactivity through habits practicable anywhere.
sessions.practice: Hold one sleep anchor and one movement block for five days. Note food timing on the same log.
sessions.science: Sleep, food, and movement raise the threshold where steadiness breaks.

sessions.title: Your Steady Week
sessions.quote: Stack the small things until they hold.
sessions.scene: Nothing dramatic happened this week. He ran the pause, the leave-line, the short apology, and the sleep anchor. That is what holding looks like from inside.
sessions.in_room: You fold the course into a one-page steady week: cues, six seconds, exhale, leave-line, same-day ownership, and two boring-hour anchors.
sessions.leave_with: You leave with a written steady-week plan and one measurable marker.
sessions.practice: Complete a one-page steady-week plan with one weekly marker you will report to your facilitator or accountability partner.
sessions.science: Small repeated anchors outperform rare heroic effort.

reentry.title: Coming Home Present
reentry.lead: Twelve short film sessions for fathers in rehab or treatment preparing to reconnect with their children and/or a significant other: the body you bring home, the wave, few promises kept, the child who grew, small deposits, repair, reunion day, and the season after. Built so a man can complete the practices inside the rules that govern him now.
reentry.desc: Twelve short sessions on presence after time in a program: reconnect with children and a significant other.
reentry.fine1: Self-paced film. Twelve weeks. One short film each week, then a checkpoint and a lived practice. Watch when you can. A Certified Facilitator is available when your seat is claimed.
reentry.fine2: Logged sessions and a checkable practice. Completion never requires contact with your child, and no practice ever asks you to go beyond the rules that govern you now or any court order. Where contact is limited, every drill has a before-return option.

welcome.title: Start here
welcome.ken: Coming home is not the same as being present. If you are in rehab or treatment, or standing in that stretch before you reconnect with your child or a partner, this is for you. Presence is a skill. It is how you show up without making the people you love pay for the pressure you carried.
welcome.micah: I built this path so you can finish it. Each week is one short film, a few questions, and a small practice you can do inside the rules that govern you now. This practice never requires contact with your child. I will walk it with you. Here's session one.

sessions.title: The Body You Bring Home
sessions.quote: Your body did its job there. Now teach it that home is not there.
sessions.scene: Quiet hours in the treatment house. A door slams down the hall. Before a thought arrives, his shoulders are up and his eyes are on the doorway. Same body that will walk into a loud kitchen on his first night home.
sessions.in_room: The body's alarm in plain language: how a long stretch in a controlled environment (program or facility) retunes it, and how that collides with a loud home and a waiting significant other. You plot your baseline and pick your tells.
sessions.leave_with: You can name what your body is doing when it revs, and call it a physical response, not a character flaw.
sessions.practice: Keep a short body-state log and name two likely home triggers.
sessions.science: Fight or flight can outlast the threat; naming the response is the first retraining step.
sessions.before_return: Keep a three-times-daily one-word body-state log where you are now. Name two likely home triggers (kids, partner, kitchen noise). Rehearse the sentence you will use to tell family what helps.
sessions.after_return: Keep the log at home, agree one signal with a family member if contact allows, and report what happened.

sessions.title: Home Is Not There
sessions.quote: Same noise, new meaning. Train the difference.
sessions.scene: On the house phone he hears a shout in the background. His body tags it as danger. On the next early leave pass he labels the same sound: kid looking for a shoe. Same noise. New meaning. Shoulders stay down.
sessions.in_room: You train the difference between there (program rules, high alert) and home with concrete sounds and scenes. Rehearsal gives the body a new meaning before the live test.
sessions.leave_with: You can catch a home sound and label it as home on purpose.
sessions.practice: Name two home sounds that used to mean threat and rehearse a calm home label for each.
sessions.science: Retraining meaning reduces false alarms when old cues meet a safe setting.
sessions.before_return: List two sounds or scenes from home (kids, partner, street) and write the new meaning next to each. Rehearse the labels aloud daily for five days inside program rules.
sessions.after_return: When one of those sounds hits, say the home label once under your breath and log whether your body stood down.

sessions.title: Plan Around the Wave
sessions.quote: Plan around the wave. Do not grade yourself by it.
sessions.scene: Day nine after his first overnight pass. He slept badly, snapped over spilled cereal, and by noon he is quietly deciding he is failing his kids and his partner. He is not failing. He is in a wave, and the plan says what to do on wave days.
sessions.in_room: Energy, mood, and sleep run in waves in the early weeks of any return from a program. That is expected. You plan around it instead of reading it as a verdict on the reconnect.
sessions.leave_with: You can expect the low weeks, plan around them, and stop grading yourself by them.
sessions.practice: Write a wave-day rule: sleep anchor, fewer commitments, and one recovery move.
sessions.science: Early-return waves in sleep and mood are common while a body leaves an imposed routine.
sessions.before_return: Hold one fixed sleep and wake time for five nights in the house. Write your wave-day rule on one page for kids and partner contact.
sessions.after_return: Hold the same sleep anchor at home and use the wave-day rule on the next hard day.

sessions.title: Few Promises, Kept
sessions.quote: Few commitments, kept without fail.
sessions.scene: He wants to promise everything on the first call home. He picks two standing call times the program phone will allow, and keeps both. By week three his child and his significant other stop asking if he means it.
sessions.in_room: Distance and early return punish over-promising. You choose a short list you can keep from where you actually are (program rules, court orders), then keep it without fail.
sessions.leave_with: You can make fewer promises and keep every one you make.
sessions.practice: Choose at most three commitments you can keep this week and keep a written record.
sessions.science: Reliability beats volume; each kept promise is evidence.
sessions.before_return: Make and keep up to three small promises deliverable inside your current rules. Where no contact is permitted, keep promises to your facilitator or cohort and file the child- and partner-facing list for day one.
sessions.after_return: Keep three small specific promises in a week at home and log each one.

sessions.title: The Child Who Grew
sessions.quote: Meet the child in front of you, not the one you left.
sessions.scene: On a permitted call from the house, the child talks about a teacher he has never heard of and a best friend whose name is new. He left a child who held his hand crossing the street. He meets the one on the line now.
sessions.in_room: You map where your child actually is now against the child you left, then build questions that rebuild a current picture: friends, fears, interests. You also note what your significant other has been carrying.
sessions.leave_with: You can recalibrate to the child who exists today.
sessions.practice: Build a one-page current picture and draft questions that are only questions.
sessions.science: Children hit growth milestones on a clock; knowing the present child is the base of attunement.
sessions.before_return: Build a one-page current picture from photos, letters, and what others report. Draft ten questions with no advice attached. Paper is the pass. A permitted call can use them later.
sessions.after_return: Hold one ten-minute questions-only conversation. Log three things you learned.

sessions.title: Ask Before You Assume
sessions.quote: Ask once. Listen longer than you talk.
sessions.scene: On the first visit, he almost fills the silence with advice for his partner and his child. He asks one real question instead, then shuts up long enough to hear the answer. They talk more in two minutes than in the last month of lectures.
sessions.in_room: Assumptions belong to the people you left. You practice one clean ask and a longer listen with your child and/or significant other, then reflect one thing you heard.
sessions.leave_with: You can ask once and listen longer than you talk.
sessions.practice: Ask one real question and reflect one thing you heard without fixing.
sessions.science: Listening longer than you talk rebuilds a current map of the child and the home.
sessions.before_return: Write one real question. Rehearse listening longer than you talk. Paper is the pass. Where a permitted call exists, you may ask it there.
sessions.after_return: Ask one question in person, listen longer than you talk, and log what you reflected back.

sessions.title: Small Deposits
sessions.quote: Small and often beats big and rare.
sessions.scene: Mid-conversation with his significant other on an early leave pass, the child appears holding a drawing. He stops, looks at it, and says show me the best part. Twenty seconds. That is a deposit.
sessions.in_room: Trust rebuilds through many small responsive interactions with kids and partner, not one big make-up moment. You practice catching and returning bids for attention.
sessions.leave_with: You can make daily small deposits and explain why they beat grand gestures.
sessions.practice: Catch and return three bids, or role-play five exchanges if contact is limited.
sessions.science: Serve and return: a child's bid met by a steady adult builds trust and brains.
sessions.before_return: Write a 60-second settling routine on paper and rehearse it. Catch and return bids on paper or with a cohort partner. Paper is the pass. Use it before a permitted call if you have one.
sessions.after_return: Settle first, then run five exchanges a day for a week and tally them.

sessions.title: Frequency Beats Intensity
sessions.quote: Show up short and steady.
sessions.scene: He used to wait for a perfect long visit after discharge. He switches to short, on-time calls the program schedule allows. The child starts setting a place for the call without being asked. His partner stops bracing for a miss.
sessions.in_room: Predictable short contact beats rare dramatic presence. You design a frequency you can keep from where you stand: program phone rules, court orders.
sessions.leave_with: You can show up short and steady on a schedule the child and partner can trust.
sessions.practice: Set one repeatable short contact ritual inside the rules that govern you now.
sessions.science: Predictability lowers a child's background stress more than occasional intensity.
sessions.before_return: Build the ritual on paper and file it for day one. That is the pass. Where current rules allow a short contact, you may run it.
sessions.after_return: Run the short ritual twice from home in one week and keep the times exact.

sessions.title: When It Breaks
sessions.quote: Rupture is normal. Repair is the skill.
sessions.scene: He promised a call at seven. The house phone line ran long and the call went out at nine. The next call opens with the repair to his child and his partner, said plainly, no excuses attached.
sessions.in_room: Every close relationship ruptures. Repair, not perfection, builds security with kids and a significant other. You practice a plain repair script until it comes out steady.
sessions.leave_with: You can come back after a bad moment and repair it out loud.
sessions.practice: Write a repair for one past rupture and rehearse it aloud.
sessions.science: Reliable repair, not perfection, is what builds security.
sessions.before_return: Write the repair for one past rupture in your own words, whether or not it can be sent. Rehearse it aloud with a cohort partner or facilitator.
sessions.after_return: Perform one deliberate repair after a rupture and record what you said.

sessions.title: Repair Without Pride
sessions.quote: Go first. Keep it short.
sessions.scene: Pride wants him to wait for his significant other to cool off after a hard call. He goes first instead: I was wrong to raise my voice. You did not deserve that. Short. No defense. The air changes.
sessions.in_room: You practice going first with a short repair toward your child and/or partner. Pride delays the skill; going first protects the bond.
sessions.leave_with: You can go first with a short repair when pride wants to wait.
sessions.practice: Write a go-first repair in under twenty words and deliver or rehearse it.
sessions.science: Going first models responsibility; delay teaches the other person to carry the silence.
sessions.before_return: Write a go-first repair in under twenty words. Rehearse until it is steady. Deliver through a permitted channel if allowed, otherwise file it.
sessions.after_return: Go first on the next miss. Keep it short. Log the words.

sessions.title: Reunion Day
sessions.quote: If the child pulls away, that is the start, not the answer.
sessions.scene: First hour home after the program. The younger one hides behind a leg. The older one shrugs off the hug. His significant other is careful, not cold. He keeps his voice low and offers the small plan he rehearsed: a walk to the corner and back, nothing more.
sessions.in_room: You prepare for the first hours back with kids and/or a significant other, including early pull-away. You write and rehearse a low-pressure first-hour plan.
sessions.leave_with: You leave with a realistic, rehearsed first-hour plan and the patience to let it be imperfect.
sessions.practice: Write and rehearse a low-pressure first-hour plan.
sessions.science: Early pull-away at reunions is common and often temporary; patience is a skill.
sessions.before_return: Write the low-pressure first-hour plan (kids and/or partner) and rehearse it aloud. Your facilitator checks the plan.
sessions.after_return: Run the plan and report how it went.

sessions.title: The Season of Return
sessions.quote: The return is a season, not a day.
sessions.scene: Week six after discharge, an ordinary Tuesday. Nothing dramatic happened. He did the ritual with the kids, checked in with his partner, logged the wave, made the small deposit. That is the plan working.
sessions.in_room: You fold the course into a personal return plan for fathering and partner reconnect, frame the work as a long season, and name an accountability partner.
sessions.leave_with: You leave with a written season plan, a first checkpoint, and a named accountability partner.
sessions.practice: Complete a one-page return plan with a checkpoint date and named accountability partner.
sessions.science: Routines hold gains; steady spaced practice beats bursts.
sessions.before_return: Complete the one-page return plan, name the accountability partner, and set the first after-return checkpoint date.
sessions.after_return: Work the plan and report at the checkpoint.

coparenting.title: Same Team
coparenting.eyebrow_track: BUILT FOR FATHERS RAISING CHILDREN ACROSS TWO HOMES
coparenting.lead: Twelve short films on co-parenting as one team for your children: cool the heat, keep messages businesslike, and hand off with a calm ritual.
coparenting.desc: Twelve short sessions on co-parenting across two homes: one team, a shared goal, flooded means pause, businesslike messages, reliability, and the handoff ritual.
coparenting.fine1: Self-paced. Twelve weeks. One short film each week, then a checkpoint and a lived practice. A Certified Facilitator is available when your seat is claimed.
coparenting.fine2: Completion never requires contact with your child. No practice asks you to go beyond the rules that govern you now or any court order.

welcome.title: Start here
welcome.ken: Your child does not need you and their other parent to be a couple. They need you on the same team. That is a skill: keep the child at the center when the old fight wants the mic.
welcome.micah: I built this path so you can finish it. Each week is one short film, a few questions, and a small practice you can actually do. I will walk it with you. Here's session one.

sessions.title: One Team for the Children
sessions.quote: Whatever we are to each other, we are one team for the child.
sessions.scene: A parent-teacher meeting. The two adults sit one seat apart, not touching, not fighting, and both sign the same plan for the same child. The child sleeps easier that night.
sessions.in_room: What being on one team means when the adults may not be together, with the child's experience at the center.
sessions.leave_with: You can state the shared frame in child-centered terms.
sessions.practice: Write one child-centered team sentence and keep it where you will see it before hard contact.
sessions.science: A child caught between adults carries the load in his body; one shared frame lowers it.

sessions.title: Write the Shared Goal
sessions.quote: One child-centered sentence you can both hold.
sessions.scene: He wants a ten-point manifesto. He writes one sentence instead: We keep school nights calm so she can sleep and learn. That sentence steers the next hard text.
sessions.in_room: You draft one child-centered goal sentence clear enough to hold when heat rises. Agreement on everything is not required.
sessions.leave_with: You have one child-centered sentence you can both hold.
sessions.practice: Write one shared-goal sentence. Send it through a permitted channel, or file it to send when allowed.
sessions.science: One clear goal steers hard moments better than a stack of demands.

sessions.title: Flooded Means Pause
sessions.quote: Flooded means pause. Then come back.
sessions.scene: The message thread heats up and he can feel his heartbeat in his ears. He names the pause, puts the phone face down, and walks. Later he comes back, and the conversation works.
sessions.in_room: When your heart is racing, the thinking brain goes offline. You train recognizing flood, pausing, then coming back.
sessions.leave_with: You can recognize flooding in yourself and pause before you make it worse.
sessions.practice: Rehearse the pause rule once. Use it on any heated exchange this week and log both ends.
sessions.science: Past a racing heartbeat nobody absorbs a word. Pause. Come back when you can think.

sessions.title: Break Clean
sessions.quote: Break off clean. Name when you will resume.
sessions.scene: He almost ghosts the thread. Instead he writes: I am flooded. Let's resume at 8 tonight. At eight he shows up. The topic survives because the break was clean.
sessions.in_room: You practice a short break-off script that names the pause and the resume time. No speech. No slam.
sessions.leave_with: You can break off clean and resume when you said.
sessions.practice: Write a clean break-off line with a resume time. Use it once on a heated call or thread.
sessions.science: Naming the resume turns a pause into a trustworthy reset.

sessions.title: Businesslike
sessions.quote: Short, factual, about the child.
sessions.scene: Three lines. Pickup Friday at five. Homework due Sunday. Doctor confirmed Tuesday. Nothing about the past. The reply comes back the same way.
sessions.in_room: Brief, factual, child-focused communication. Where the adults are not together, the low-contact model that keeps heat out of the channel.
sessions.leave_with: You can send a businesslike message that carries only what the child needs.
sessions.practice: Draft three businesslike messages. Send whichever a permitted channel allows; file the rest.
sessions.science: Less adult heat in the channel lightens what the child carries.

sessions.title: Cooler Channels
sessions.quote: Use the channel that lowers heat.
sessions.scene: The text thread is a furnace. He moves the logistics to a written log and saves voice for a scheduled call after a pause. The facts still move. The heat drops.
sessions.in_room: You choose channels on purpose. Some media raise heat before a word is read. Cooler channels protect the child from spillover.
sessions.leave_with: You can pick the channel that lowers heat for logistics and hard topics.
sessions.practice: Name your hottest channel and your cooler backup. Move one real logistics item to the cooler channel this week.
sessions.science: Medium matters; channel choice can prevent a fight before content does.

sessions.title: Reliability Buys Trust
sessions.quote: Trust is bought with reliability.
sessions.scene: For a month he is never once late for the agreed call, never once asks for an exception. Nobody says anything. The tone in the messages changes anyway.
sessions.in_room: How a parent earns caregiving trust through small kept promises over time. Encouragement follows the track record.
sessions.leave_with: You can earn trust in steps with small reliability.
sessions.practice: Identify one small reliable act and do it consistently for a week. Log it.
sessions.science: Reliability, repeated, is what reopens the gate.

sessions.title: Never Against an Order
sessions.quote: Never ask a child to carry an adult fight, and never against an order.
sessions.scene: He wants an exception. He wants the child to pass a message. He does neither. He keeps the written plan exactly. Trust grows inside the line, not against it.
sessions.in_room: Court orders and agreements are the floor. Trust is earned inside them, never against them. Children are never messengers for adult fights.
sessions.leave_with: You can operate inside any legal boundary and keep adult conflict off the child.
sessions.practice: List the rules that govern you now. Choose one small act of compliance you will keep perfectly this week. Never use the child as a messenger.
sessions.science: Trust built against an order is not trust; it is risk the child pays for.

sessions.title: What the Child Carries
sessions.quote: The child carries the distance. Lighten the load.
sessions.scene: Every week the child leaves one home with a bag. He learns what is hard about the bag and fixes his end: the charger, the book, the jacket for the colder house.
sessions.in_room: Your child's experience of moving between two homes, the load at the transition, and the warmth that builds resilience regardless of the arrangement.
sessions.leave_with: You can see the transition through the child's eyes and lighten one concrete load.
sessions.practice: Ask one open question about moving between homes if contact allows, or file it. Fix one logistics friction on your side.
sessions.science: Transitions are stress points; warm, practical help lightens what the child carries.

sessions.title: Two Homes, One Child
sessions.quote: Predictable rules beat perfect agreement.
sessions.scene: The houses will never match perfectly. He stops fighting for identical rules and makes his own home predictable: bedtime, homework, phone off at dinner. The child stops guessing.
sessions.in_room: Perfect agreement is rare. Predictable rules at your place give the child ground to stand on even when the homes differ.
sessions.leave_with: You can run a few clear, predictable rules the child can count on at your place.
sessions.practice: Write three predictable rules for your parenting time. Post them where you will follow them.
sessions.science: A child can adapt to two homes when each home is steady.

sessions.title: The Handoff
sessions.quote: Predictable beats perfect.
sessions.scene: Same spot, same time, a calm two-minute handoff. Within a month the child stops going quiet on the ride there. Nothing was said. The routine said it.
sessions.in_room: A predictable handoff carries the child's things, the practical facts, and a calm goodbye. Old disputes stay off the curb.
sessions.leave_with: You can run a predictable handoff that keeps adult heat away from the child.
sessions.practice: Write your handoff checklist: place, time, items, facts, goodbye. Rehearse once.
sessions.science: The handoff is where the child feels the team most directly.

sessions.title: The Handoff Ritual
sessions.quote: Same place, same time, same calm script.
sessions.scene: Bag, jacket, homework. See you Thursday at five. Same script every week. The child starts handing over the bag before anyone asks.
sessions.in_room: You lock a short ritual: same place, same time, same calm script. You leave with a one-page plan and a first checkpoint.
sessions.leave_with: You leave with a repeatable handoff ritual and a first checkpoint.
sessions.practice: Complete a one-page handoff ritual plan and walk it through with a cohort partner or facilitator. After return, execute one handoff to the plan and log it.
sessions.science: A predictable ritual says what words cannot at the transition.

fundamentals.title: Fathering Fundamentals
fundamentals.eyebrow_track: SEVEN SECRETS · ASSESSMENT & COURSE · ALREADY FILMED
fundamentals.lead: Dr. Ken Canfield's Seven Secrets course, already filmed: intro + seven secrets. Free assessment included.
fundamentals.desc: The Seven Secrets of Effective Fathers: intro + seven secrets, with shape previews and practice checkpoints on the guide page.
fundamentals.fine1: Self-paced film. A Certified Facilitator is available when your seat is claimed.
fundamentals.fine2: Logged sessions and checkpoints for enrolled learners. Guide-page checkpoints are practice only and never mint a certificate on their own.

welcome.title: Start here
welcome.ken: These are the Seven Secrets I have taught fathers for decades. Short sessions you can use the same night. Not a theory class. A way to be the man your child can count on.
welcome.micah: I built this path so you can start tonight. Each session is short. Watch, take the questions if they are there, try one move at home. I will walk it with you. Here's session one.

sessions.title: Introduction
sessions.quote: Welcome, overview, and take the assessment.
sessions.scene: A dad opens the course, hears the welcome, and takes the assessment before the first secret.
sessions.in_room: Course welcome, overview film, and free assessment entry point.
sessions.leave_with: You know the arc of the seven secrets and have started the assessment.
sessions.practice: Complete the free assessment before Session 1.
sessions.science: Assessment first so growth targets are personal, not generic.

sessions.title: First Secret: Commitment
sessions.quote: Present physically, emotionally, spiritually; commitment builds trust.
sessions.scene: He chooses to be present in the room, in the conversation, and in the spiritual lead of the home.
sessions.in_room: Commitment as physical, emotional, and spiritual presence; trust as the fruit.
sessions.leave_with: You treat presence as a commitment your child can feel across all three dimensions.
sessions.practice: Name one physical, one emotional, and one spiritual way you will show up this week.
sessions.science: Commitment builds trust and lays the foundation for lasting influence.

sessions.title: Second Secret: Knowing Your Child
sessions.quote: Unique personality, needs, and interests open deeper connection.
sessions.scene: He names what makes this child different and asks a question that fits that child, not a script.
sessions.in_room: Personality, needs, and interests as the path to meaningful connection.
sessions.leave_with: You can name concrete traits, needs, and interests for each child.
sessions.practice: Write a one-page profile of who this child is now (personality, fears, current passions, next six months), with the mother or caregiver if that channel is safe. No visit required.
sessions.science: Understanding uniqueness opens the door to deeper connection.

sessions.title: Third Secret: Showing Up Consistently
sessions.quote: Stability through consistent actions, values, and discipline.
sessions.scene: Week after week he keeps the same actions and values so the home feels steady.
sessions.in_room: Stability via consistent actions, values, and discipline.
sessions.leave_with: You treat consistency as security your child can feel.
sessions.practice: Pick one action, one value, and one discipline habit you will keep the same this week.
sessions.science: Children thrive on stability; consistency builds confidence.

sessions.title: Fourth Secret: Protecting and Providing Security
sessions.quote: Physical, emotional, and spiritual safety and provision.
sessions.scene: He meets a need and removes a threat so the child feels safe and valued.
sessions.in_room: Safety and provision across physical, emotional, and spiritual dimensions.
sessions.leave_with: You can name how you protect and provide in each of the three dimensions.
sessions.practice: Name one protective move and one provision move you will make this week.
sessions.science: Protection and provision communicate value to the child.

sessions.title: Fifth Secret: Loving Their Mother
sessions.quote: Honor their mother. Civil if you are not together. Never undercut her.
sessions.scene: On an ordinary day he almost talks their mother down within earshot. He stops. The child will not hear him undercut her, even if the adults are not a couple.
sessions.in_room: How he speaks about their mother. Honor her. Civil if you are not together. Never undercut her. Not a couple-therapy session.
sessions.leave_with: You have one sentence you will not say about their mother, and a civil child-only note if the coparent channel is safe.
sessions.practice: Write one sentence you will not say about their mother this week. If a coparent channel is safe, send one short civil note about the child. If it is not, keep the sentence in your notes.
sessions.science: Children should not have to choose a side or hear you tear her down.

sessions.title: Sixth Secret: Active Listening
sessions.quote: Two-way. Full attention. Not an interrogation.
sessions.scene: On an ordinary day he puts the phone face down. One real conversation with a program peer, a coparent, or a call he already has. After, he writes what they actually said, not what he planned to say.
sessions.in_room: Active listening is two-way, with full attention, not an interrogation. The usual rival is the phone.
sessions.leave_with: You can put the phone face down, hear them out, and say back what you heard.
sessions.practice: Put the phone face down for one real conversation this week (program peer, coparent, a call you already have). After, write what they actually said, not what you planned to say.
sessions.science: Full attention is the skill. Advice can wait.

sessions.title: Seventh Secret: Spiritual Equipping
sessions.quote: Live convictions a child can trust.
sessions.scene: He names one conviction and lives it in the open at work, in the program, or at home. He keeps his word.
sessions.in_room: Spiritual equipping here means grounded convictions you live. Kids watch what you live.
sessions.leave_with: You leave with one conviction you will live in the open this week.
sessions.practice: Name one conviction you will live in the open this week at work, in the program, or at home. Keep your word.
sessions.science: Kids watch what you live.
